To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

distinct alterations in brain connectivity are observed in Parkinson's disease, in response to dopamine medications, and that these alterations are differentially associated with different motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.

(a) Parkinson's disease ON and OFF dopamine have distinct connectivity changes, (b) these connectivity changes are associated with specific motor symptoms, and (c) the connectivity changes in Parkinson's disease are different than those in healthy controls.
distinct brain connections are altered in Parkinson's disease and with dopamine, and some of these are associated with specific motor symptoms.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between brain circuitry and motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease.
understanding the neural mechanisms underlying the motor symptoms of Parkinson's disease and how dopaminergic medications may affect these symptoms.
understanding the relationship between brain connectivity changes and specific motor manifestations of Parkinson's disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dopaminergic medication state connectivity changes are different from the disease state connectivity changes, but both are different from the healthy state.
the medication-state and disease state connectivity are distinct and the medication-state connectivity is not a simple normalization of disease-state connectivity.
dopaminergic medication drives distinct alterations in brain connectivity and these alterations are associated with the improvement of specific motor symptoms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

Parkinson's medication-state connectivity changes are not simply ‘normal’ or ‘abnormal’ but distinct from each other and from healthy control connectivity, and these medication-state connectivity changes may or may not be associated with improved motor function.
dopaminergic therapy induces distinct alterations in brain connectivity that are related to specific motor manifestations in Parkinson's disease.
dopaminergic medication induces unique connectivity changes, only a subset of which relate to improved motor function.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the brain connectivity changes associated with Parkinson's medications and Parkinson's disease are distinct.
the brain connectivity changes associated with Parkinson's medication-state are not simply ‘normalized’ versions of the disease-state changes but rather are unique.

dopaminergic medication does not simply ‘normalize' abnormal connectivity associated with Parkinson’s disease, but rather dopaminergic medications drive unique changes in connectivity that only partially relate to motor symptom improvement.
